First of two mechanisms producing the illusion: the medium becomes perceptually transparent, an 'open window' (FE).
Second mechanism: the medium is perceptually transformed into an independent social entity (FE).

Presence as 'social actor within medium': media users respond to social cues from on-screen/virtual personas as if the interaction were mutual, though it is one-sided (FAITHFUL-Lombard&Ditton, citing Horton & Wohl 1956).
Presence as 'medium as social actor': users respond to social cues from the medium itself, per Nass and colleagues' 'computers are social actors' research program (FAITHFUL-Lombard&Ditton).
The illusion of self-motion experienced when presence is evoked alongside rapid point-of-view movement (FE).

A kind of motion sickness -- dizziness, eyestrain, disorientation, dysphoria, standing/walking unsteadiness, nausea -- resulting from presence combined with illusory movement (FAITHFUL-Lombard&Ditton, citing Biocca 1992; Kennedy et al. 1993).
'You are there' / 'it is here' transportation subtypes: user transported to a mediated place, or objects/people from elsewhere transported into the user's environment (FAITHFUL-Lombard&Ditton).
Presence as social richness (social presence theory, media richness theory) plus the 'we are together' shared-space transportation subtype (FAITHFUL-Lombard&Ditton).
Presence as immersion: perceptual submersion of the senses (HMD, headphones, gloves) plus a psychological component of involvement/absorption/engrossment (FAITHFUL-Lombard&Ditton).

Interactivity explicated via five subsidiary variables (inputs accepted, modifiable characteristics, range of change, input-response correspondence, response speed) as a primary causal variable for both mechanisms of presence (FAITHFUL-Lombard&Ditton).
Presence as realism, split into perceptual realism (objects/people look/sound/feel real) and social realism (plausible, 'true to life' content) (FAITHFUL-Lombard&Ditton).
Vection and simulation sickness identified as physiological effects of presence combined with illusory movement (FAITHFUL-Lombard&Ditton).
Enjoyment named 'perhaps the most prominent psychological impact of presence,' linked to the commercial popularity of presence-evoking technologies (FE).

'Involvement' effect (fun, exciting, competitive, addictive, intense) reported as the highest-rated factor (8.7/10) in Heeter's 1995 BattleTech VR-entertainment survey (FAITHFUL-Lombard&Ditton, reporting Heeter 1995).

Skills training: flight-simulator and ARI virtual-navigation-training studies cited as evidence high-presence media improve trained performance over low-presence alternatives, with explicit transfer-risk caveats (FAITHFUL-Lombard&Ditton).

Memory and social-judgment effects: presence-enhancing conditions linked to greater source-monitoring error, misattributing fictional mediated information to real-world judgments (FAITHFUL-Lombard&Ditton, reporting Ditton 1997).
Presence explicitly framed as a property of the person, not the medium, occurring or not at each instant of media use rather than varying continuously in degree (FE).
